🔴 **Major** · `f-b54113f9` · conventions · CONFIRMED

The new drift-vs-regression rule (3) asserts that one benchmark out of line with its siblings is necessarily a code regression, but three of the five benchmarks pin `today=_TODAY` and two read the real clock, so the two can diverge from the three with no code change at all.

**Failure scenario.** CLAUDE.md:200-202 now states: 'One benchmark out of line with its four siblings is a code regression however slow the runner was.' In tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py, test_bench_assemble_brief_context (:107), test_bench_build_plan_section (:128) and test_bench_daily_snapshot (:133) all pass `_TODAY.isoformat()` explicitly, while test_bench_get_training_plan_progress (:116) and test_bench_get_training_plan_status (:121) call `handler({})` and window on `date.today()`. The three pinned targets therefore do a fixed amount of work forever; the two unpinned ones do more work every day. Measured above: the progress payload alone grew 5,447 -> 9,946 chars between the baseline-capture date and the CI run quoted as evidence, worth +3.18% on identical code. So the exact shape the rule cites as proof of a code regression (assemble_brief_context -0.34% beside get_training_plan_progress +13.86%) is also the shape calendar drift produces here, and the new rule tells the next reader to stop looking. It is being written into CLAUDE.md as a durable rule, which is where a wrong one costs the most.

> fleet-wide: it moves all five together. One benchmark out of line with its
>   four siblings is a code regression however slow the runner was

Fixed in c577f1fed4c5 — was read as runner drift and re-run to green. Unlike the latency axis,
    this one has no `benchmark` fixture, so it is the INVERSE of that axis'
